title: Waltzes, polkas, quadrilles and street tunes of the early days
summary: Dance repertoire of his youth, played mostly by ear; tunes such as Tiger Rag and a tango remembered by the interviewers.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What we played: tunes and repertoire in the early days

blocks.x: Yeah, you can hear. Mr. Garland, you were talking about the sequence of tunes that you were playing. You said first you played waltzes?

Oh yeah, during that time we played waltzes, pox shots, we played shotties, and we played mazookas. Now when you played those- Then we used to play quadrilles, which people say Lancer, but written with quadrilles. You didn't call them figures set. They called figures no answers, you know. Lancer? Yeah, they called it now the- Square dance? Square dance. Square dance. But did you play those things by ear or were you reading when you played polkas and mazookas or something? Oh, I played them by ear. By ear? No. Some bands played by music because they had different pieces they used.

By ear, I wouldn't play nothing by music. Yeah. What were they singing in the streets? What was the music? That, you know, like- Oh, yeah. Oh, well, they used to play like Tagal Rag and all that stuff and they used to play, uh, Cold Black Shine and-
Cold Black Shine and- Cold Black Shine and- Cold Black Shine and- Yeah, yeah. Oh, yeah. Shine and-
Mm-hm- I was trying to think, it was far back, old numbers you know. Pete called Sonora, beautiful number. Was that a tango? Something like that.

You know what that's called? That's called the Egyptian fantasy. That's what Bechet called the Egyptian fantasy, that Tunger's singing. What he called it now? Da-dee-dee-do-dee-dee-da-da. He called the Egyptian. Isn't that the Egyptian? Egyptian. That's the middle part, that's the bridge. No, no, no, no. That's the Egyptian, isn't it? Yeah. It's a beautiful tune.
